name: 7:3 Repeaters (20 mm)
description: Intermittent hangs on a 20 mm edge: 6 reps of 7 s on / 3 s off per set, 3 min between sets, at 60-70 % of max total load. Develops forearm capillarisation and oxidative recovery between contractions.
cues: Stop the set if grip position degrades
source: Lattice Training fingerboard methodology; López-Rivera & González-Badillo (2012) Sports Technology 5:100-110; Medernach et al. (2015) J Strength Cond Res 29:3093-3102

name: Max Hangs 10 s (20 mm)
description: Single 10 s hangs on a 20 mm edge at 80-90 % of max total load with full 3 min recovery. Maximises neuromuscular recruitment of the finger flexors with low metabolic fatigue.
cues: Load so the last 2-3 s are hard but clean
Full 3 min rest - this is strength, not endurance
source: Lattice Training fingerboard methodology; López-Rivera & González-Badillo (2012) Sports Technology 5:100-110; Hörst (2016)

name: Density Hangs (20 mm)
description: Long 30 s low-intensity hangs (~50-55 % max) to accumulate time-under-tension for connective-tissue conditioning during capacity phases.
source: Lattice Training density hangs; Baar K. (2017) Sports Med 47(Suppl 1):5-11 (tendon loading)

name: ARC Traversing (Aerobic Restoration & Capillarity)
description: Continuous easy climbing for 20 min at a pump level of 3-4/10. Builds local aerobic capacity and recovery between hard moves.
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016)

name: Limit Bouldering
description: 4-6 boulders at or near your maximum grade, 3-5 quality attempts each, with 3 min rest between attempts. Builds maximal recruitment and movement skill.
cues: Mix steep, crimpy and dynamic styles
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016); Lattice Training

name: 4x4 Boulder Circuits
description: Four boulders climbed back-to-back (one set), rested 4 min, repeated 4 times. Classic anaerobic power-endurance protocol.
cues: Minimal rest between problems within a set
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016)

name: Route Intervals
description: Climb a route 2-3 grades below onsight level, rest an equal time to climbing time, repeat. Builds lactate tolerance and route-length endurance.
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016)

name: Campus Board Ladders
description: Explosive ladder moves on a campus board (1-3-5 etc.) with full recovery. Advanced contact-strength and rate-of-force-development training; only for climbers with years of finger training.
cues: Only when fresh and fully warmed up
Stop at first sign of finger or elbow pain
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016); Lattice Training

name: Performance Climbing / Projecting
description: Low-volume, high-quality attempts on goal routes or boulders. Used in the taper/peak phase to express fitness gained.
source: Hörst E. Training for Climbing, 3rd ed. (2016)

name: Weighted Pull-ups (Volume)
description: 4 sets of 6 at ~75 % of max total load (bodyweight + added). Builds pulling muscle cross-section in the capacity phase.
cues: Full hang to chin over bar
source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41:687-708)

name: Weighted Pull-ups (Max Strength)
description: 5 sets of 3 at 85-90 % of max total load with 3 min rest. Neural strength development for lock-offs and steep climbing.
source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41:687-708)

name: Explosive Pull-ups
description: Bodyweight pull-ups performed with maximal intent, aiming to pull the chest to the bar. Develops rate of force development.
source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41:687-708); Hörst (2016)

name: Overhead Press
description: Standing barbell or dumbbell press. Antagonist work to balance the pulling-dominant shoulder of climbers.
cues: Bar path close to the face
Finish with biceps by the ears
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor; ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41:687-708)

name: Weighted Dips
description: Parallel-bar dips with added load as tolerated. Strengthens triceps and anterior shoulder for mantles and press moves.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Deficit Push-ups
description: Push-ups from parallettes or plates allowing the chest to drop below the hands, increasing scapular range of motion.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Reverse Wrist Curls
description: Light dumbbell wrist extensions to strengthen the forearm extensors and reduce lateral elbow overuse risk.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Tuck Front Lever Holds
description: Isometric tuck front lever holds on a bar or rings. Builds straight-arm scapular depression and trunk tension for steep terrain.
cues: Back flat, hips level with shoulders
source: Hörst (2016); progressive calisthenics

name: Advanced Tuck / Straddle Front Lever
description: Harder front lever progressions (flat back advanced tuck, one leg or straddle) held for 8 s.
cues: Progress lever length only with clean form
source: Hörst (2016)

name: Front Lever Raises
description: From hang, raise a straight (or tucked) body to front lever position and lower slowly. Dynamic trunk power.
source: Hörst (2016)

name: Dragon Flag Negatives
description: Lying on a bench holding behind the head, lower a rigid body from vertical over 4-5 s.
cues: Weight on upper back, not neck
source: Progressive calisthenics; Hörst (2016)

name: Hanging Leg Raises
description: Strict straight-leg raises from a dead hang to toes-to-bar or 90 degrees. Develops hip-flexor and abdominal compression for high feet.
source: Hörst (2016)

name: Hollow Body Hold
description: Supine hollow position with lower back pressed to the floor. Foundation for body tension.
source: Gymnastics conditioning literature

name: Seated Pike Compression Lifts
description: Seated with legs straight, hands beside knees, lift the heels off the floor using active hip flexion. Trains active compression for high-steps.
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: Jefferson Curl (Loaded)
description: Standing on a box with light load (start with 5-10 % bodyweight), segmentally roll down to loaded end-range hamstring and spinal flexion and roll back up.
cues: Chin to chest first, vertebra by vertebra
Start very light and progress slowly
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003); Afonso et al. (2021) Sports Med 51:1305 (strength training vs stretching for ROM)

name: Cossack Squats
description: Lateral squat to one side with the other leg straight. Builds adductor length and single-leg strength for wide stems and drop-knees.
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: Frog Stretch (Timed)
description: Kneeling wide with shins parallel, rock hips back to stretch the adductors. Improves turnout and hip-to-wall positioning.
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003); ACSM Guidelines (2021): 30-60 s static holds

name: Middle Split Progression
description: Horse-stance to wall-supported middle split. Use contract-relax (PNF): 5 s adductor contraction then sink deeper.
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: 90-90 Hip Opener Holds
description: Seated with front and back legs at 90 degrees. Hold internal and external hip rotation each side.
cues: Hinge forward over the front shin
Switch sides when the beep sounds
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: Couch Stretch (Hip Flexors)
description: Rear knee against a wall, front foot planted: stretches rectus femoris and hip flexors for high-step and heel-hook positions.
cues: Squeeze glute of the back leg
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: Pancake Stretch (Loaded)
description: Seated straddle folding forward with a light plate held to the chest. Develops hamstring and adductor length together.
cues: Hinge from hips, not the back
source: Kurz T. Stretching Scientifically, 4th ed. (2003)

name: Wall Slides
description: Back to the wall, slide arms overhead while keeping contact. Trains scapular upward rotation and posterior tilt.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Prone Y-T-Ws
description: Lying prone, lift arms in Y, T and W shapes. Strengthens lower trapezius and rotator cuff.
cues: Squeeze shoulder blades down and back
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: German Hangs
description: Hang from rings or a bar with arms behind the body for shoulder extension mobility. Feet supported to control load.
cues: Keep feet on the floor to start
source: Gymnastics conditioning; Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Open-Book Thoracic Rotations
description: Side-lying with knees bent, rotate the top arm open to the floor. Restores thoracic rotation for reaches and flagging.
cues: Follow your hand with your eyes
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Banded External Rotations
description: Elbow at the side bent to 90 degrees, rotate the forearm outward against a light band. Rotator-cuff prehab.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Scapular Pull-ups
description: From a dead hang, depress and retract the scapulae without bending the elbows. Trains active shoulder engagement before hard pulling.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: Doorway Pec Stretch
description: Forearm on a door frame at shoulder height, step through to stretch pectorals that tighten from climbing posture.
source: Vagy J. Climb Injury-Free (2016), The Climbing Doctor

name: 5 s Max Hang Test (20 mm)
description: After a thorough warm-up, work up in load to the heaviest clean 5 s hang on a 20 mm edge (half-crimp). Record the added weight (negative if assisted).
source: Lattice Training fingerboard methodology; López-Rivera & González-Badillo (2012) Sports Technology 5:100-110

name: Weighted Pull-up 1RM Test
description: Work up to the heaviest single strict pull-up (chin over bar from a dead hang). Record the added weight.
source: ACSM Position Stand: Progression Models in Resistance Training (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41:687-708)
